evidence.claim: Forest roads pass the remnants of an ironmaking community
evidence.quote: This National Forest Scenic Byway weaves through a landscape of diverse vegetation, scenic views, unique geological formations and an abundance of wildlife. In addition, there are numerous historic places-the remnants of a once thriving mining community.

evidence.claim: Highlands Scenic Byway is a National Forest Scenic Byway in Virginia, listed by FHWA as a 20-mile drive taking one hour before trail stops.
evidence.quote: Highlands Scenic Byway • Virginia Length 20 mi / 32.2 km Time to Allow 1 hour to drive the byway, but take several hours to enjoy the trails offered.

evidence.claim: FHWA highlights its vegetation, geological formations and remains of a mining community.
evidence.quote: This National Forest Scenic Byway weaves through a landscape of diverse vegetation, scenic views, unique geological formations and an abundance of wildlife. In addition, there are numerous historic places-the remnants of a once thriving mining community.

evidence.claim: Longdale Furnace’s industrial story began in 1827, when John Jordan and John Irvine built Lucy Selina Furnace, named for their wives.
evidence.quote: Industrial activity began here in 1827 when Lexington builder and entrepreneur John Jordan and his partner John Irvine built a coal-blast iron furnace here which they named Lucy Selina Furnace after their respective wives.

evidence.claim: William Firmstone and Ario Pardee bought the operation in 1869 and redeveloped it as a hot-blast, coke-fired furnace.
evidence.quote: was purchased in 1869 by William Firmstone and his partner Ario Pardee. They redeveloped the site as Virginia’s foremost hot-blast coke-fired furnace

evidence.claim: Workers’ dwellings and managers’ houses grew beside the operation; the company dissolved in 1914.
evidence.quote: A community of workers’ dwellings, managers’ houses, and related buildings sprang up to service the activity. The company was dissolved in 1914.

evidence.claim: At Longdale Furnace, the historic district includes the original stone furnace stack, the company office and laboratory, and two tall brick chimneys.
evidence.quote: It includes the original stone furnace stack (1827), two-story Longdale Iron Company Office (late-1820s), Longdale Iron Company Laboratory, two tall cylindrical brick chimneys

evidence.claim: From the Longdale Furnace exit, the Forest Service describes a climb on SR 770 to North Mountain’s trail access at Forest Road 447.
evidence.quote: Take the Longdale Furnace exit #35 and travel south for 0.34 miles to SR 770. Turn Left and go 4.1 miles to the top of the mountain

evidence.claim: Recreation.gov describes a loop returning to Forest Road 447 along North Mountain Road.
evidence.quote: Drive northeast on North Mountain Road until you return to Forest Road 447.

evidence.claim: North Mountain’s trail access at Forest Road 447.
evidence.quote: Beginning at North Mountain at the intersection of Forest Road 447 and State Route 770

evidence.claim: The original stone furnace stack at Longdale dates to 1827.
evidence.quote: the original stone furnace stack (1827)

evidence.claim: John Jordan and John Irvine named their furnace Lucy Selina after their wives.
evidence.quote: John Jordan and his partner John Irvine built a coal-blast iron furnace here which they named Lucy Selina Furnace after their respective wives.

evidence.claim: The business passed to Jordan’s sons before Firmstone and Pardee bought it in 1869.
evidence.quote: The operation was continued by Jordan’s sons but was purchased in 1869 by William Firmstone and his partner Ario Pardee.

evidence.claim: Their redevelopment brought a hot-blast coke-fired operation under the Longdale Iron Company name.
evidence.quote: They redeveloped the site as Virginia’s foremost hot-blast coke-fired furnace named the Longdale Iron Company.

evidence.claim: Longdale’s district includes workers’ dwellings, managers’ houses and buildings that served the ironmaking operation.
evidence.quote: A community of workers’ dwellings, managers’ houses, and related buildings sprang up to service the activity.

evidence.claim: The inventory identifies a company laboratory, machine shop and doctor’s office, as well as the two-story company office.
evidence.quote: two-story Longdale Iron Company Office (late-1820s), Longdale Iron Company Laboratory, two tall cylindrical brick chimneys, brick machine shop, Firmstone-Johnson House (1870s–1880s), the Queen Anne-style Assistant Manager's House (1870s–1880s), and the Company Doctor's Office.

evidence.claim: Many buildings disappeared after the company dissolved in 1914, but Virginia’s Department of Historic Resources describes surviving traces of the industrial village.
evidence.quote: The company was dissolved in 1914. Many of the buildings disappeared but the Longdale Furnace Historic District still maintains a vestige of its former character.

evidence.claim: At Forest Road 447 and SR 770, North Mountain Trail heads southwest along the mountain with occasional views east and west.
evidence.quote: Beginning at North Mountain at the intersection of Forest Road 447 and State Route 770, south of the radio tower, the trail heads southwest along North Mountain and offers occasional views to the east and west.

evidence.claim: The Civilian Conservation Corps built the trail in the 1930s.
evidence.quote: The trail was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930’s

evidence.claim: The Forest Service rates it difficult.
evidence.quote: Trail Difficulty: Difficult

evidence.claim: Snow and ice make the FR 447/SR 770 trailhead difficult to reach in winter.
evidence.quote: The trailhead at Forest Road #447 and State Route #770 is difficult to access in the winter months because of snow and ice accumulations on the road surfaces.
